_comment: DOJ-derived test set. Each fraud case is a SYNTHETIC reconstruction of a fraud typology that appears in publicly reported U.S. Department of Justice business-email-compromise (BEC) prosecutions and in FBI IC3 / DOJ guidance on BEC. No real victim data is used: the messages are written from scratch against this repository's three seeded vendors so the reconstructions are checkable, deterministic and safe to commit. The 'note' on each case names the typology and the public source it is drawn from. Legitimate cases ('control_*') are routine traffic plus the two intended frictions (a first-time vendor, a genuine bank change), so the set measures false positives as well as catch rate. LIMITATION: these are reconstructions written by someone who knows what Doris checks, so they are cleaner than real traffic and the catch rate here is an upper bound, not a field estimate. Run: python -m detector --offline evaluate --testset detector/testset/cases_doj.json
_sources: U.S. v. Evaldas Rimasauskas, S.D.N.Y. (2017-2019): forged invoices and letters impersonating a real supplier (Quanta Computer) diverted over $100M from Google and Facebook.
U.S. v. Obinwanne Okeke, E.D. Va. (2020): conspiracy to commit wire fraud; roughly $11M lost to business email compromise; 10 years.
U.S. v. Ramon Olorunwa Abbas, C.D. Cal. (2022): business email compromise and laundering of fraudulent wire transfers; 11 years.

FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3): Business Email Compromise; the 'vendor email compromise' and 'business executive impersonation' typologies, the five BEC categories, and the annual loss figures IC3 publishes (BEC has repeatedly been the costliest reported category).

U.S. Department of Justice / FBI public guidance on BEC: spoofed or lookalike sender domains, compromised vendor mailboxes, free webmail impersonation of a known contact, reply-to pivots, requests to change remittance/bank details, urgency tied to a payment deadline, and requests to confirm by replying to the same email.
